Sample text:
---
*On Embers*

The fire went out around ten, but at midnight my brother's backyard still smelled like it.

He had fallen asleep in a lawn chair with a cooling beer in his hand. The dog was asleep too, curled against his leg. The marshmallows were gone except for one that had melted onto a stick and hardened into something like white plastic. I stayed up because bugs were doing something interesting in the fence, and because I didn't want to be the first person to actually go inside and admit the night was over.

I poked the coals with a stick. Not because I wanted to start the fire again — it was too late for that, and nobody was left awake to enjoy it — but because I couldn't help it. A red pulse showed itself under the gray ash, then dimmed, then showed itself again where the stick had shifted things.

That's the thing about embers. A flame is all performance. It sings, it crackles, it throws light across faces, it demands marshmallows exactly this dark and no darker. An ember does none of that. It just sits there, mostly gray, mostly quiet, and holds heat in a place you can't see until you touch it. You can step on one barefoot in the morning and learn about physics and regret at the same time.

I think that's why we keep poking them. It's not hope that the fire will come back. It's a kind of memory-work. You want to know if it's still warm inside.

Later, walking back to the house, I passed the field beyond the fence where the fireflies were blinking. No heat at all, just light, made for no reason I could tell. Jellyfish do that in the deep ocean. So does the moon, it borrows it. So does a phone screen at 2 a.m. in a dark bedroom. There are a lot of ways to glow without burning, and we don't talk about them as much because burning is more dramatic.

A person, I suspect, is more ember than flame most of the time. The big bright parts — the graduation, the first kiss, the job you got, the argument that actually changed something — those flare up and then they go. What's left is a long, low warmth: the way a certain song still steadies your breathing, the way you can still hear your grandmother saying your full name when you're in trouble, the way an old friend can text "you up?" from another time zone and it feels like nothing has cooled at all.

Embers are patient in a way fires aren't. A fire needs feeding. An ember just needs not to be rained on. You can leave it for hours and come back and, if you blow gently — not hard, hard just scatters it — it will remember it used to be a flame and sort of be one again, for a minute.

I went inside eventually. My shoes smelled like smoke the next morning in the kitchen, and my brother's wife said, "Did you stay up all night?" and I said, "Sort of," because I was carrying the backyard with me to the coffee maker and didn't want to explain that I'd spent an hour not reviving the fire, just checking that it hadn't completely let go yet.

That's the ember trick, I guess. It leaves without really leaving.

Its pathos comes less from loss than from the wish to check whether warmth is still there: the speaker pokes the coals without trying to revive the fire, and carries the scene indoors rather than explaining it. The piece invites the reader to recognize enduring attachments in ordinary traces—a song, a grandmother’s voice, a friend’s late text—without making them grand or dramatic.
